221) I take this claim—which is, in any case, absolutely indisputable—“on trust,” without proof. Proving it, if that is even possible, is a task for Cosmology, and perhaps for Ontology. Phenomenology, by contrast, insofar as it is anthropology, “proves” only what concerns human beings as human beings. The “physical” death of a human being is caused by biological, and therefore natural, processes. Phenomenology does not discuss these. It simply accepts them as “axioms” that do not need to be proved within its own field. Phenomenology will, however, discuss “free” death—for example, suicide and the conscious “risk” of one’s life. For our present purposes, though, it is enough to accept that human beings are finite in general: that their bodies are mortal and that they cannot free themselves from them.

223) From the Hegelian-Marxist point of view, human history comes to an end. In other words, humanity eventually exhausts its historical possibilities. At first sight, this seems to imply that a human being can no longer be a person, or be free.

This is precisely what bourgeois “liberals” and “individualists” accuse Hegel and Marx of. They insist that the historical process must be limitless—and therefore that no true knowledge of it can ever be possible, a point that matters greatly to them.
But this argument rests on a misunderstanding.
First, the historical process does not repeat itself. It ends, once and for all, with communism. In this sense, historical humanity taken as a whole can itself be called an “individual.”

Second, history does not exhaust all human possibilities. On the contrary, Marx speaks of a “leap from the realm of necessity into the realm of freedom,” a leap that occurs at the end of history. Once human beings have exhausted their historical possibilities—that is, their social and political possibilities—they still possess infinitely many “personal” or “individual” possibilities, which they will in fact realize under communism.

And if humanity should one day perish—for example, because the Sun dies—it will perish without having exhausted all of its possibilities. This is why some people speak of moving to another planet, and so on.

Third, Marx—and Marx alone—understands that historicity, precisely because its possibilities are limited, restricts human freedom and individuality. Bourgeois “individualists” therefore have nothing to teach him on this point.
225) Of course, “free decisions” do not make up the whole of a person’s life. On the contrary, they are extraordinarily rare, and sometimes entirely absent.

But if someone never “makes a decision,” then, if you like, he is not really a “human being” in the relevant sense. In any case, he remains purely “thetic,” and his future can be predicted, because he is nothing more than the result of what is already present in him. Nothing essentially new will then arise.
Conversely, wherever something genuinely new does arise, it cannot be predicted. But once we know what that new thing is, we can deduce everything that came before it.

In either case, we can go back beyond A. Y was itself once the negation of X, and so on. The chain therefore always leads back to the “first human being,” which means to the first appearance of the dialectical entity as such, and thus ultimately to its non-dialectical origins.

In this sense, one might say that human beings are always free, since refusing to change can itself be a free acceptance of what is given.
Strictly speaking, however, this is not correct. Merely continuing what already exists cannot be called “free” in the strongest sense.

If one prefers, we can distinguish two kinds of freedom. The first is the free decision whether or not to be “free”—that is, the choice between negating what is given and accepting it. The second is the actual negation of what is given.
228) Except, of course, by choosing points that lie along the path already travelled.

Human historicity rules out literally “repeating the path already travelled.” Even if a human being—or humanity—returned to a state that had existed before, the new state would still differ from the first because it would include the memory of the first, and that memory is not identical with the first state itself.

Bergson rightly observed that although the ball on a roulette wheel may keep repeating one and the same movement, the same is not true of a person walking around a table. Each circuit places that person in a new situation. The first time, he knows he is doing it for the first time. The second time, he knows he has already done it once, and so on.

229) To desire an end while rejecting the means—to choose a destination while refusing to travel along the only road that leads to it—is the defining feature of “utopia” and, ultimately, of “madness.”
This will be discussed in the Phenomenology itself.
230) In Plato and Kant, and more generally in philosophy in the strict sense—that is, in Cosmology and Ontology—the question takes the following form:
“How must the existing world, and Being itself, be constituted for the world to be able to ‘appear’ to human beings in experience exactly as it actually appears?”

With regard to humanity and history in particular, philosophy—that is, Cosmology—asks what human beings must be, and what their history must be like, for them to “appear” as they do at a given historical moment.
Phenomenology, by contrast, never goes beyond the limits of these “appearances.” It asks instead:
“How must the world, humanity, and history have appeared to human beings in the past for them finally to ‘appear’ as they do now?”
But these appearances are just as human as human beings themselves. The law governing their relation to one another is therefore the same law that governs actual history: it is dialectical.

For example, if we establish that it is raining, or that it has rained, we know that the road will be wet. But if the road is wet, that does not prove it rained. Someone may have sprayed it with water, and so on.

Its “geometrical genesis” therefore does not coincide with its “logical genesis.”
233) The same applies to the communism of the future.

Phenomenology can certainly say certain things about it as a possible historical appearance. But it cannot say with certainty that communism will actually be realized. Its realization depends on free action—that is, on a revolutionary struggle that cannot be predicted.
Just as we cannot predict the activity that consciously aims at communism, neither can we predict the exact character of its result: communist society itself.

In this sense Marx speaks of a “leap from the realm of necessity into the realm of freedom,” emphasizing that until this leap has actually taken place, there is very little we can say about what lies beyond it.
A “scientific” historical prediction can deal only with the thetic elements of history: the development, “in the normal course of things,” of something that already exists in an embryonic form.

Revolutionary change itself, however, cannot be predicted. Once a revolution has begun, we may be able to predict its course—that is, the way it develops—because this development also proceeds “thetically.” But we cannot predict the original emergence of the revolutionary break itself.
234) Here we encounter the “logical circle” once again. See p. 234 ff.
We can fully understand the past only by understanding the present. But we cannot fully understand the present without understanding the past.

The phenomenologist’s method—the method that makes it possible to write a Phenomenology—therefore consists, if you like, in moving repeatedly from the present back to the past and from the past forward to the present, gradually clarifying each by interpreting it through the other.
Within the Phenomenology itself, however, the method amounts to a straightforward description of the historical process once that process has been understood in a certain way.
As the work proceeds, this “understanding” of the process makes it possible to select the appropriate material, and also to schematize and idealize what has been selected.
235) This “deduction” is, of course, a posteriori. See above, p. 408 ff.
236) What has just been said implies that only true philosophy can be circular. Science cannot.
Only human existence is dialectical, together with what is contained within it—in particular, the knowledge that human beings have of the world.

But science deliberately “abstracts” from the fact that all knowledge is human. When science speaks about the world, it excludes the human being to whom that world is “given”—that is, the human being to whom it “appears.”
The object of science is therefore not dialectical. And for the same reason, science—even “true” science—is not circular.
237) This is where the essential difference between philosophy and science lies.
Science always has “axioms,” without which it could not exist. But it cannot “prove” those axioms—that is, it cannot demonstrate their “universality and necessity.”
238) We can picture the system as a circle made up of circles.
Ontology completes the full circle of ontological description and returns to its starting point. From there, the next step leads into the cosmological description of nature.
This description is not circular but linear, because nature is not dialectical. It leads instead to the emergence of the human being.
From that point, the cosmological description of humanity traces another complete circle. When it returns to its starting point, it passes into Phenomenology.
Phenomenology then completes its own circle and passes back into Ontology, and so on.
239) Hegel’s error cannot be used as an argument against the criterion of circularity.
First, this is because Hegel’s system is not in fact circular; it only appears to be. Second, his mistake is less significant than it first seems.
He simply attributed to Napoleon’s Empire what in reality applies only to an International Union of Soviet Republics.

In other words, his mistake was merely chronological—or, put differently, he failed to identify exactly what had happened in 1806. In a certain sense, he anticipated the future. But what he anticipated was not itself mistaken.

This is why, in my own presentation of the Phenomenology, I pass over the French Revolution and Napoleon. The “appearance” Hegel had in mind exists in a much more complete form and is expressed far more clearly today.

Everything essential that has happened between 1806 and our own time is already present in Hegel’s Phenomenology, including, in particular, fascist “racism.” In this sense, Hegel was right to speak of the circularity of his Phenomenology.

I too am “anticipating” when I treat the worldwide socialist revolution as though it had already been accomplished. But there is a very good chance that this anticipation will prove correct, whereas the construction of a worldwide classless society by Napoleon was historically impossible.

But the chronological gap between 1806 and 1917 does not correspond to any gap in the Phenomenology. What was essentially new during that period—democratic liberalism—had already been described by Hegel in Chapter V.

247) Because the antithesis contains negation—that is, negativity or freedom—it cannot be predicted.
The emergence of communism is therefore not necessary. It depends on revolutionary struggle, on a free effort that may very well never occur.

And since the concrete content of the antithesis is determined by the unpredictable character of the negation of the thesis, we cannot know the concrete content of communism in advance with any precision.
We can nevertheless know that communism “negates” socialism while also “preserving” it and “raising it to a higher level.” And in the present case, as we will now see, that is enough.
It is important to emphasize that the final completion of socialism requires uninterrupted effort and action. It requires both work and struggle.

Every philosophical stage—every thesis, antithesis, and synthesis—is, so to speak, dialectical “through and through.” Within each stage we must therefore distinguish further sequences of dialectical triads, which means further sequences of antitheses—that is, of creative and revolutionary actions.
If even one such action fails, the whole process “comes to a halt.”

In practical terms, this means that the process can move more or less quickly depending on the intensity of the work and struggle devoted to it. But once a stage has already begun, only chronological changes of this kind remain possible.
Without the appropriate creative and revolutionary actions, socialism would never have appeared. Indeed, it might never have appeared; something entirely different might have arisen in its place.
But since socialism has appeared, it will either be brought to completion in a fully determinate way or the historical movement will come to a complete stop.
Effort is therefore necessary for one reason only: to prevent this halt and to accelerate the process.
